summary.text: A Howard Swan parkland course on the western Algarve, opened on 1 January 2002 a short drive from the old town of Lagos.

setting.text: Offers views over the Bay of Lagos to the east and the Monchique mountains to the north.
Sits a 10-minute drive from the old walled town of Lagos, at the mouth of the Bensafrim River.
The course has two sections: a Resort section (holes 1 to 3 and 13 to 18) and a Country section (holes 4 to 12).
Fairways on the opening and closing holes weave around clusters of residential housing.
Holes 6, 7 and 8 sit in the south-west corner at the highest part of the course and form a triangular loop that uses the natural contours.
On the back nine the holes generally descend towards the clubhouse.
The resort's own description says the later holes drop to an area of streams, lakes and arched bridges.
The resort says the Atlantic is visible from most holes.
The Bela Colina Village townhouses sit between the 3rd, 13th and 14th holes.
Natural vegetation, ravines and water hazards all come into play, according to National Club Golfer.

history.text: Designed by Howard Swan, a past president of the European Institute of Golf Course Architects.
Swan's stated philosophy was to build a course as if it had always been there, preserving and blending with the natural terrain.
The routing moves south towards the Atlantic before turning for home, with the final holes running north.

trivia.text: Top100golfcourses entered Boavista in its 2026 Top 50 for Portugal at number 40.
National Club Golfer placed it 108th in its Top 100s list of European golf resorts.
Today's Golfer lists it as par 71 and 6,675 yards.
Today's Golfer said in its review that the par 3s are terrific and called the par-4 7th the top hole.
The course has a replica of the Swilken Bridge from the 18th hole at St Andrews.
Water comes into play on holes 14, 15 and 17, which Portugalgolf calls the lake holes.
The resort has a short game area with three greens, one for putting, one for chipping and one ringed by bunkers, plus a driving range.

1.text: A meandering downhill par 4, lined with sub-tropical planting and the resort's properties.

6.text: A par 3 needing a tee shot over a natural ravine; National Club Golfer says it plays over 210 yards from the back tees and also needs a wall in front of the green carried.

7.text: A par 4 and the course's signature hole, with the Atlantic as backdrop and panoramic views.

8.text: A par 5 where the ravine comes into play again; National Club Golfer calls it the hardest hole on the front nine.

14.text: A par 3 playing over 245 yards from the back tees, with a lake in front and another to the right of the green, according to National Club Golfer.

15.text: A right-doglegged par 4 of 390 metres that Top100golfcourses regards as the toughest hole on the card.

16.text: Water hazards come into play here, as on the 15th and 17th.

17.text: A par 4 with water, which National Club Golfer describes as one of the more picturesque holes on the property.

18.text: A 418-metre par 4 that veers right off the tee to a heavily bunkered green, which Top100golfcourses says should not be underestimated.

local.text: Lagos sits at the mouth of the Bensafrim River on the Atlantic, and had a 2021 census municipality population of 33,494.
Lagos was a centre of the Age of Discovery and a frequent home of Henry the Navigator; John I assembled his fleet there before the 1415 attack on Ceuta.
Much of old Lagos was destroyed by the 1755 earthquake and tsunami, though some 16th-century walls and the governor's castle remain.
The nearby Ponta da Piedade rock formations are among Lagos's main sights.
Faro airport is roughly 55 miles east along the coast.
Palmares and Penina are both within about half an hour's drive.
